caps_pedrera.kg_context:
Element: Chimneys and rooftop sculptures ('caps')
Creator: Antoni Gaudí
Timeline: Built as part of the roof during the main 1906-1910 construction phase; later restored to remove post-Gaudí chimneys, TV antennas, and other later additions.
Purpose: Every piece on the roof does a job: the chimneys extract smoke from the apartments below, the vents renew the building's air, the discharge domes handle drainage, the skylight towers are the exits of the staircases, and some of those towers also house the water tanks. Their sculptural treatment is applied to elements that are functional first.
Inspiration: Nicknamed the 'garden of warriors' by poet Pere Gimferrer, since the grouped chimneys look like helmeted sentinels standing guard over the skylight/staircase exits; their helmet-like silhouettes are sometimes linked to Gaudí's interest in medieval fortress architecture.
materials: brick; lime coating; broken marble; broken Valencia tiles; glass (one chimney)
construction_process: Built from brick and coated with lime, broken marble, or glass; all pieces are functional (smoke extraction, ventilation, drainage) rather than purely decorative, despite their sculptural appearance.
Chimneys: 28, in several groupings
Skylight staircase exits: 6
Vents: 2
Discharge domes: 4
- The roof holds 28 chimneys in several groupings, 6 skylight/staircase exits, 2 half-hidden vents that renew air inside the building, and 4 discharge domes -- all functional rather than purely decorative.
- Some staircase-exit towers double as housings for the building's water tanks, a few of which are snail-shaped.
- One chimney is topped with glass -- reportedly added by Gaudí the day after the building's inauguration party using empty champagne bottles, later restored with early-20th-century champagne-bottle bases.
---
Part of: Casa Milà (La Pedrera)
Creator: Antoni Gaudí, commissioned by Pere Milà and Roser Segimon
Context: Gaudí designed the house as 'a constant curve, both outside and inside,' combining ruled geometry with naturalistic form. There is no agreement on which mountain inspired the facade -- candidates proposed by different contemporaries include the rocks of Fray Guerau in the Prades mountains, St. Miquel del Fai, the Torrent de Pareis cliffs in Menorca, Uçhisar in Cappadocia, and Mola Gallifa.
---

casa_batllo.kg_context:
Element: Casa Batlló
Creator: Antoni Gaudí (the 1904-1906 remodelling, with Domènec Sugrañes i Gras, Josep Canaleta and Joan Rubió); original building by Emili Sala Cortés (1877); commissioned by Josep Batlló i Casanovas
Timeline: The original building was built in 1877 for Lluís Sala Sánchez; bought by the Batlló family in 1903; Gaudí was hired in 1904 and the work finished in 1906; sold to the insurer Seguros Iberia in 1954; the outer balconies were restored in 1983 and the facade lit in 1984; bought by the Bernat family (Chupa Chups) in 1993; the noble floor opened to the public in 2002; declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
Purpose: A remodelling rather than a new build: Josep Batlló wanted the 1877 apartment block turned into a home for his family on the noble floor with rental flats above, and into a showpiece that would outshine its neighbours on the Illa de la Discòrdia. It has been open to the public as a house-museum since 2002.
Inspiration: Commissioned at the height of the rivalry between the bourgeois families of Passeig de Gràcia (the 'Illa de la Discòrdia', the Block of Discord): the textile industrialist Josep Batlló wanted a house that would put the neighbouring buildings by Puig i Cadafalch and Domènech i Montaner in their place.
materials: Montjuïc sandstone; trencadís (ceramic mosaic); coloured glass discs; polychrome ceramic (330 pieces); wrought iron
construction_process: Not a new build but a remodelling: Gaudí persuaded Batlló not to demolish the 1877 building and to transform it instead; the central light well was enlarged and new floors added.
Noble floor area: over 700 m²
Catenary arches in the attic: 60
- The attic has sixty catenary arches, creating a space that evokes the ribcage of an animal.
- The central light well is clad in tiles in graded shades of blue (deeper at the top, lighter at the bottom) to spread light evenly between floors.
- Its popular name 'Casa dels Ossos' (House of Bones) comes from its biomorphic, skeletal look.
- The arched roofline evokes the back of a dragon or dinosaur; a common reading casts the cross-topped tower as the lance of Saint George driven into the beast's back.
- There is a popular legend, unconfirmed by documentary sources, that the Sagrada Família (then under construction) could once be seen through the small triangular window in the roof; in 2022 it was confirmed that the towers are partly visible from that point today.
---
Related: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) as Park Güell, Casa Milà and the Sagrada Família; part of the Illa de la Discòrdia alongside other notable Modernista buildings (not by Gaudí).
---
Related: Trencadís used here as on the Park Güell dragon, the serpentine bench and the Casa Milà rooftop chimneys.

catenaria_pedrera.kg_context:
Element: Espai Gaudí attic (catenary/parabolic brick arches)
Creator: Antoni Gaudí (arches marked on site by builder Bayó and foreman Canaleta)
Timeline: Built during the main 1906-1910 construction phase, as the attic laundry/drying space beneath the roof.
Purpose: The attic was built as the building's shared laundry and drying floor, and its arches carry the undulating roof and rooftop terrace above the apartments. It now houses the Espai Gaudí exhibition on Gaudí's work.
Inspiration: The rippling roofline is widely compared to the ribs of a huge animal or the fronds of a palm; the space, now called Espai Gaudí, is often described as feeling like walking through the inside of a whale's ribcage.
materials: brick (volta catalana / timbrel vaulting)
construction_process: Each arch's profile was set on site with a hanging-chain (catenary) model: nails were driven at the two spring points of the arch, a chain hung between them so its lowest point matched the desired deflection, and that traced curve became the template for the brick vault -- the same method Gaudí used at Casa Batlló and, earlier, on the roof of the Mataró workers' cooperative ('L'Obrera Mataronense').
Arch count: 270 parabolic brick arches
Arch spacing: about 80 cm apart
- Built using volta catalana (Catalan/timbrel vault) technique -- thin layered brick vaulting imported from Italy in the 14th century, laid without a full wooden centering framework.
- Arch height and spacing directly follow the courtyards' footprint below: arches rise higher where the plan narrows and drop lower where it widens, so the roof structure encloses the irregular figure-8 courtyard shape beneath it.
- 270 parabolic brick arches of varying height, spaced about 80 cm apart, give the roofline a rippling, organic silhouette.

There is no agreement on which mountain inspired the facade -- candidates proposed by different contemporaries include the rocks of Fray Guerau in the Prades mountains, St. Miquel del Fai, the Torrent de Pareis cliffs in Menorca, Uçhisar in Cappadocia, and Mola Gallifa.

cupula_sagrada_familia.display_name: Crossing Vaults and the Tower of Jesus Christ
cupula_sagrada_familia.kg_context:
Element: Crossing Vaults and the Tower of Jesus Christ
Creator: Antoni Gaudí
Timeline: The central nave vault was completed in 2000; the crossing structure and its great hyperboloid have been under construction since the early 2000s; the Tower of Jesus Christ was structurally completed on 20 February 2026.
Inspiration: Gaudí wanted a visitor standing at the main entrance to see the nave, crossing and apse vaults rising in ascending perspective.
materials: post-tensioned stone
construction_process: The crossing rests on four central porphyry columns carrying one great hyperboloid, ringed by two circles of twelve smaller hyperboloids.
Crossing vault height: 60 m
Apse vault height: 75 m
Tower of Jesus Christ height: 172.5 m
- Hyperboloid forms become more pronounced in Gaudí's later design work, particularly from 1914 onwards.
- At 172.5 m, the Tower of Jesus Christ made the Sagrada Família the tallest church in the world, 11 m above the previous record holder, Ulm Minster.
---
Part of: Sagrada Família
Creator: Antoni Gaudí (architect from 1883); begun by Francisco de Paula del Villar; driven by the bookseller José María Bocabella
Context: Conceived as an 'expiatory temple' funded only by private donations, inspired by the basilica of Loreto after Bocabella's 1872 trip to the Vatican; it combines Gothic forms with Gaudí's own curvilinear Art Nouveau.

Creator: Antoni Gaudí
Timeline: Built as part of the main terrace/entrance works, documented as complete by the January 1903 Anuari de l'Associació d'Arquitectes description of the site.

materials: trencadís (tile-shard mosaic); masonry/mortar core

Element: Nativity Facade
Creator: Antoni Gaudí
Timeline: Built between 1893 and 1936, before work was interrupted by the Civil War; it is the oldest facade and the one most directly shaped by Gaudí. Declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005 together with the crypt.

Creator: Antoni Gaudí
Timeline: Built during the main 1906-1910 construction phase; restored from 1987 onward, including rejoining fallen stone pieces sourced from the Villefranche quarry.
Purpose: The facade carries only its own weight, so it works as a self-supporting envelope rather than as structure: with the loads taken by the iron beams behind it, the front can open into large windows and balconies and the interior partitions can be moved freely without touching the building's stability.

construction_process: Large limestone blocks were cut to follow the projection of Gaudí's model, then raised into place and adjusted to align in a continuous curve with the surrounding pieces; the facade connects to curved iron floor beams rather than load-bearing walls.

la_pedrera.kg_context:
Element: Casa Milà (La Pedrera)
Creator: Antoni Gaudí, commissioned by Pere Milà and Roser Segimon
Timeline: Commissioned September 1905; presented to Barcelona City Council February 1906; pre-existing building demolished and construction begun 1906; completed December 1910; certificate of completion issued October 1912; declared a historic/artistic monument in 1969; UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984; headquarters of Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera since 2013.
Purpose: Built as a mixed-use apartment block: the Milà family lived on the noble floor and the four upper floors were let as rental apartments, over a ground floor and basement designed for vehicle access. It stopped being a private residence when it was taken over for other uses, and since 2013 it has served as a cultural centre and the headquarters of the Fundació Catalunya La Pedrera, open to visitors.
Inspiration: Gaudí designed the house as 'a constant curve, both outside and inside,' combining ruled geometry with naturalistic form. There is no agreement on which mountain inspired the facade -- candidates proposed by different contemporaries include the rocks of Fray Guerau in the Prades mountains, St. Miquel del Fai, the Torrent de Pareis cliffs in Menorca, Uçhisar in Cappadocia, and Mola Gallifa.
materials: limestone (Garraf Massif, lower floor; Villefranche quarry, upper floors); wrought iron; curved iron floor beams
construction_process: Gaudí's last private residence commission; the pre-existing building on the plot was demolished (unlike the Casa Batlló renovation) and the new self-supporting stone facade, connected to curved iron floor beams, was built 1906-1910.
Floor area: 1,323 m² per floor
Plot area: 1,620 m²
Storeys: 9 (basement, ground floor, mezzanine, main/noble floor, four upper floors, attic)
- Self-supporting stone facade with no load-bearing walls, connected to curved iron beams surrounding the perimeter of each floor -- allowing interior walls to be added or removed without affecting the building's stability.
- In August 1908 the City Council fined the project for exceeding its permitted height and site boundaries; the dispute was resolved in December 1909 when the building was certified as monumental and exempted from strict bylaw compliance.
- Nicknamed 'La Pedrera' ('the stone quarry') by residents who disliked its rough-hewn, undulating stone facade -- an insult that became its popular name.
- Considered a predecessor of later biomorphic buildings such as the 1921 Einstein Tower (Erich Mendelsohn), the Guggenheim Museum (Frank Wright), and Frank Gehry's Disney Concert Hall.
---

Creator: Antoni Gaudí, commissioned by Eusebi Güell
Timeline: Commissioned 1900 as a private residential development; built 1900-1914 (works abandoned with only 2 of 60 planned houses built); sold by Güell's heirs to Barcelona City Council in 1922; opened as a municipal park in 1926; declared an artistic monument in 1969; UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984.

Creator: Antoni Gaudí
Timeline: Remodelled between 1904 and 1906.
Purpose: The street facade is the building's public face, the part that had to win the rivalry of the Illa de la Discòrdia, and it works as display as much as enclosure. construction_process: The facade divides into three integrated sections: the ground floor and galleries in undulating sandstone, the multicoloured central part with its balconies, and the upper crown, a great gable that conceals the old water tank.
Polychrome ceramic pieces: 330
- The upper crown carries a frieze of ceramic pieces open to various readings; Gaudí reused trencadís fragments left over from other works.
- The metallic-finish roof tiles mimic the scales of a monster, shading from green (where the head begins) to blue and violet in the centre, and to red and pink at the far left.

sagrada_familia.kg_context:
Element: Sagrada Família
Creator: Antoni Gaudí (architect from 1883); begun by Francisco de Paula del Villar; driven by the bookseller José María Bocabella
Timeline: Begun on 19 March 1882 under Villar (a neo-Gothic design); Gaudí took over in 1883 and radically transformed it; work was interrupted and the plans partly destroyed in the Civil War (1936); resumed from reconstructed plans in 1940; consecrated as a basilica by Pope Benedict XVI on 7 November 2010; the Nativity facade and the crypt were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005; the Tower of Jesus Christ was structurally completed on 20 February 2026 and inaugurated by Pope Leo XIV on 10 June 2026.
Inspiration: Conceived as an 'expiatory temple' funded only by private donations, inspired by the basilica of Loreto after Bocabella's 1872 trip to the Vatican; it combines Gothic forms with Gaudí's own curvilinear Art Nouveau.
materials: Montjuïc stone (early phases); stone from the Withnell quarry, England (from 2018); post-tensioned stone (later construction phases); Venetian glass mosaic (pinnacles)
construction_process: The crypt was begun by Villar in a standard neo-Gothic style; Gaudí redesigned the whole from 1883; construction was slow and funded only by donations; a fire in 1936 destroyed part of the workshops and the original plans, later reconstructed from photographs and documentation; computer-aided design (CAD/CNC) has been used since the 1980s, accelerating the pace of work.
Tower of Jesus Christ height: 172.5 m
Central nave vault height: 45 m
Crossing vault height: 60 m
Apse vault height: 75 m
Column grid spacing: 7.5 m
Spires planned in total: 18
Spires completed by 2026: 14
Organ pipes installed in 2010: 1492
- The interior columns are a design unique to Gaudí: their cross-section passes from square to octagonal, then sixteen-sided and finally circular, through the intersection of helicoidal columns.
- The Passion facade contains a magic square based on the one in Dürer's Melencolia I (1514), in which the rows and columns add up to 33.
- The temple has three great facades: the Nativity (the most ornate, finished before 1936), the Passion (austere and hard-lined, sculpted by Josep Maria Subirachs) and the Glory (the largest, still incomplete).
- The spires represent, in ascending order of height, the Twelve Apostles, the four Evangelists, the Virgin Mary and, tallest of all, Jesus Christ.
- Stylistically compared to Spanish late Gothic, Catalan Modernisme and Art Nouveau; critics such as Louis Sullivan and Walter Gropius praised it, while George Orwell called it one of the ugliest buildings in the world -- matters of aesthetic opinion, not verifiable fact.
---
Related: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) as Park Güell, Casa Milà and Casa Batlló; only partly covered (the crypt and the Nativity facade) by the 2005 UNESCO 'Works of Antoni Gaudí' inscription -- unlike Park Güell and Casa Milà, which were listed in full in 1984.

House of Bones.kg_context:
Element: Casa Batlló
Creator: Antoni Gaudí (the 1904-1906 remodelling, with Domènec Sugrañes i Gras, Josep Canaleta and Joan Rubió); original building by Emili Sala Cortés (1877); commissioned by Josep Batlló i Casanovas
Timeline: The original building was built in 1877 for Lluís Sala Sánchez; bought by the Batlló family in 1903; Gaudí was hired in 1904 and the work finished in 1906; sold to the insurer Seguros Iberia in 1954; the outer balconies were restored in 1983 and the facade lit in 1984; bought by the Bernat family (Chupa Chups) in 1993; the noble floor opened to the public in 2002; declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
Purpose: A remodelling rather than a new build: Josep Batlló wanted the 1877 apartment block turned into a home for his family on the noble floor with rental flats above, and into a showpiece that would outshine its neighbours on the Illa de la Discòrdia. It has been open to the public as a house-museum since 2002.
Inspiration: Commissioned at the height of the rivalry between the bourgeois families of Passeig de Gràcia (the 'Illa de la Discòrdia', the Block of Discord): the textile industrialist Josep Batlló wanted a house that would put the neighbouring buildings by Puig i Cadafalch and Domènech i Montaner in their place.
materials: Montjuïc sandstone; trencadís (ceramic mosaic); coloured glass discs; polychrome ceramic (330 pieces); wrought iron
construction_process: Not a new build but a remodelling: Gaudí persuaded Batlló not to demolish the 1877 building and to transform it instead; the central light well was enlarged and new floors added.
Noble floor area: over 700 m²
Catenary arches in the attic: 60
- The attic has sixty catenary arches, creating a space that evokes the ribcage of an animal.
- The central light well is clad in tiles in graded shades of blue (deeper at the top, lighter at the bottom) to spread light evenly between floors.
- Its popular name 'Casa dels Ossos' (House of Bones) comes from its biomorphic, skeletal look.
- The arched roofline evokes the back of a dragon or dinosaur; a common reading casts the cross-topped tower as the lance of Saint George driven into the beast's back.
- There is a popular legend, unconfirmed by documentary sources, that the Sagrada Família (then under construction) could once be seen through the small triangular window in the roof; in 2022 it was confirmed that the towers are partly visible from that point today.
---
Related: Same architect (Antoni Gaudí) as Park Güell, Casa Milà and the Sagrada Família; part of the Illa de la Discòrdia alongside other notable Modernista buildings (not by Gaudí).
---
Related: Trencadís used here as on the Park Güell dragon, the serpentine bench and the Casa Milà rooftop chimneys.
